articles.title: Jenrick mocked after criticising Thatcher’s policies, despite naming daughter after her – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Reform UK MP says policies left a ‘deep scar’ on communities

These are from my colleague Peter Walker, who was at the Tory event where James Cleverly was named as the party’s candidate for London mayor.

Peter posted this before the result was announced.

Khan (who may or may not stand a 4th time) has thus far faced a dilettante who decided to campaign on a racist platform (Zack Goldsmith) and two oddballs in Shaun Bailey and then Susan Hall. Not even he can be lucky yet again

Interesting that [the Conservatives] did not say how many votes were cast, just the percentage - which perhaps indicates it was not a huge number

Cleverly’s speech is mainly an attack on Labour and Khan, which is likely to be a theme for his campaign: “Burnham can’t stand London and Khan stand up to Burnham.” Also a pitch about building houses and cutting crime, and boosting transport.

Cleverly says he would “end Khan’s war on motorists”, which is a sign he might lean into the anti-cycling and walking rhetoric which the London Tories have a habit of espousing. Expect talk about LTNs and 20mph zones.

In the media Q&A Cleverly is pinned down on whether he backs the Tory party line on wanting to leave the ECHR and opposes net zero. He confirms he does (as he has to). Such things will be ready ammunition for Labour.

Cleverly says of Andy Burnham, “His residual behaviour is to be anti-London”. This will very much be a theme of his campaign, it seems. Not sure how resonant a “poor London!” message will be even in London

People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place, businesses, job creators, families leaving London, and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related.

The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause.

articles.title: Iraq avoids battle with powerful militia after 'compromise' reached to hand over stronghold
articles.summary:
Iraq avoids battle with powerful militia after 'compromise' reached to hand over stronghold

Submitted by Alex MacDonald on Thu, 11/19/2026 - 12:57
Iran-backed group Kataeb Hezbollah had earlier vowed not to evacuate Jurf al-Sakhar raising fears of clashes with Baghdad
Members of Iraq's Kataeb Hezbollah ride in the back of a pickup in their stronghold in Jurf al-Sakhar in Babil Province, south of Baghdad, on 17 November (AFP/Ahmad al-Rubaye)
Off

Baghdad has agreed a "compromise" with Kataeb Hezbollah over its Jurf al-Sakhar stronghold, narrowly avoiding outright conflict between the state and the Iran-backed militia.

The powerful paramilitary group had been given a deadline of Friday to hand over control of the area in southern Iraq, with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi readying security services near the outskirts, ready to enter by force.

Officials had accused Kataeb Hezbollah of running a smuggling ring from Jurf al-Sakhar that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil.

However, three senior security officials told Reuters on Thursday that a deal had been reached that would allow Baghdad authorities to enter the town on Friday.

Lieutenant General Saad Maan, head of Iraq's Security Media Cell, said the armed group's forces would move to other areas.

A new headquarters in Jurf al-Sakhar that reports to the federal police will go into operation at 6am on Friday, under the authority of the interior ministry.

It will be led by Lieutenant General Ahmed Hatem Hamid, alongside deputy commanders Major General Hussein Ali Nassif for defence affairs, and Adi Abdel-Imam Mussah for the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF).

The deal was brokered by senior Shia political leaders, with Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran's elite Quds Force, also arriving in Baghdad late on Monday to help defuse the situation.

'Even a limited clash around Jurf could have escalated quickly, especially if other factions saw it as the start of a broader move against them'

- Hayder al-Shakeri, analyst

As recently as Tuesday, Kataeb Hezbollah - whose well-armed and well-trained forces number in the tens of thousands by their own statements - had vowed they would not leave their stronghold.

"I can state decisively and with absolute certainty that the dream they dream of the Kataeb withdrawing from Jurf al-Sakhar will not come true, not even over our dead bodies," Abu Taleb al-Saidi, a Kataeb Hezbollah commander, told AFP during a press visit to the area.

Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow with the Middle East and North Africa programme at Chatham House, told Middle East Eye there were strong incentives for everyone to avoid conflict over Jurf al-Sakher.

"But the risk was still there if Zaidi kept pushing for a change on the ground while Kataeb Hezbollah refused to shift its position. In that scenario, even a limited clash around Jurf could have escalated quickly, especially if other factions saw it as the start of a broader move against them," he said.

"The deal mattered because it gave both sides a way to step back without either appearing to fully surrender."

State crackdown

On 29 September, the US announced the withdrawal of its forces from Iraq, 23 years after the invasion that overthrew Saddam Hussein.

The pullout was tied to the disarming of the extra-government armed groups that, since the overthrow of Saddam, have been among the most powerful forces in the country.

Most of them were formed in 2014 after a call from Shia religious leader Ali Sistani to mobilise and defend the country from the Islamic State (IS) group.

But the most powerful armed groups are older and, though they officially come under the authority of the state as part of Hashd al-Shaabi, or PMF, they are effectively independent and (for the most part) loyal to Iran.

Since Saddam's overthrow the groups have established control over much of Iraqi society, with deep links to the political establishment, military and organised crime.

As the US pulls its forces out of Iraq, what happens to Iran-backed armed groups?
Read More »

Zaidi said a deadline had been set for 30 June 2027 for the groups to disarm and/or come under direct state control.

But the most powerful of these groups - Kataeb Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataeb Sayyid al-Shuhada - have already said they are unwilling to do so.

During the US-led occupation and the war against IS, the groups were responsible for killing, kidnapping and torturing thousands of Iraqis, and helped suppress the pro-democracy Tishreen movement that erupted in 2019.

In recent years, a number of them have also grouped together under the heading of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq to target Israeli and US assets over the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

Hisham al-Mozani, an activist with Al-Amal Association rights group, told Middle East Eye in September that the push to disarm the groups risked returning the country to civil war.

"For the army and security forces, maybe they will have clashes with the militias and that's a very, very dangerous thing - it will affect the economy, affect security in all of Iraq," he said.

He said he believed the process of disarming and integrating the groups would take around five years, even if the process began at all.

"Some of these militias are more than 40 years old, since the Iran-Iraq war in 1980, so they've had a long time and they're in the political parties, are present in the parliament and some of them are in the ministries," he said.

articles.title: Critics accuse The New York Times of promoting Iran war propaganda
articles.summary:
Critics accuse The New York Times of promoting Iran war propaganda

The New York Times (NYT) is facing widespread criticism over its report claiming that some of Iran's water infrastructure may have been built to support its missile programme, with critics accusing the newspaper of promoting war propaganda and providing a justification for attacks on Iranian civilian infrastructure.

Published on Monday with the headline "War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason", the article examines the geographical overlap between dam and water infrastructure projects and sites recently struck during the US-Israeli war on Iran. It suggests that some of these projects may have been designed, at least in part, to support military facilities.

One of the two journalists who wrote the piece, Sanam Mahoozi, shared the article on X, writing: “Why has Iran kept building dams amid a severe water crisis? @ErikaSolomon and I examined a striking overlap between water projects and military sites. Could some have served a dual purpose? No conclusive evidence, but questions worth exploring.”

The Iranian Water Diplomacy Association noted on Tuesday "with serious concern" the discrepancies in the report, including the fact that geographical proximity between struck sites and water infrastructure sites does not establish military use.

Read more: Critics accuse The New York Times of promoting Iran war propaganda

articles.title: Iraq strikes 'compromise' deal with Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah
articles.summary:
Iraq strikes 'compromise' deal with Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah

Iraq has reached a compromise with Kataeb Hezbollah, the Iran-backed paramilitary group, three senior security officials told Reuters, after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi readied security forces to move against the group.

Iraqi officials had accused the Iraq-based group of running a smuggling ring that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil.

Under the deal brokered by senior Shia political leaders to avert what could have been a civil war, government forces were expected to move into Kataeb Hezbollah stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, according to three security officials familiar with the deal.

Kataeb forces would move to other areas, Lieutenant General Saad Maan, head of Iraq's Security Media Cell, told Reuters.

Reflecting the gravity of the situation, Iraqi Shia political sources said Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran's elite Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad late on Monday to help defuse tensions with Kataeb Hezbollah, Tehran's most powerful militia ally in Iraq.

A spokesperson for Kataeb Hezbollah said the group's secretary-general, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, met Qaani, Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Badr Organization, another influential Iran-aligned militia, and other influential figures in a bid to prevent an escalation.

Participants described the outcome of the talks as positive in a statement issued on Thursday.

articles.title: Trump says he will 'see what happens' with Iran after 1 January
articles.summary:
Trump says he will 'see what happens' with Iran after 1 January

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Washington would "see what happens" as regards its war on Iran after 1 January.

“We're going to have a new year coming up, and we'll see what happens after January 1. But they've been nasty,” Trump told Fox News during his trip to China.

Trump made the comments during an interview in which he was asked about a CNN report that Iran was planning to detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington. A dirty bomb uses conventional explosives to spread radioactive material.

Trump downplayed such a threat, saying “I don't think so”, when asked if people in the capital should be alarmed.
